newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq allows state banks to sell hard currency.
newsitem.headline: Iraq allows state banks to sell hard currency.

text.p: Iraq, in a bid to improve its battered currency, allowed state banks to sell hard currency in exchange for dinars for the first time on Wednesday, an Iraqi senior bank official said.

"Upon orders from President Saddam Hussein, may God protect him,... we have taken new measures (to sell hard currency to people) and we have started implementation today," Zuhair Kasab, Deputy Dirctor of the state-run al-Rasheed bank told Reuters.
The Iraqi dinar surged to 1,370 against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday morning up from 1,550 on Tuesday.
The new exchange rate set by the banks was 1,340 dinar to the dollar. The price will be revised each morning, Kasab said.
"A committee was set up at the Central Bank which meets every morning and decides the rate. But it would be less than that of the commercial markets any way," Kasab said.
Traders and money changers in Baghdad said the government move to sell hard currency was aimed at improving the value of the dinar.
"A few days ago the dinar stood at 1,700 against the dollar. Now after this decision it went up to 1,370 only hours after its implementation...the dinar will gain more and more," one trader said.
They said people were queuing in front of state banks to buy dollars at the reduced prices.
Iraq at the beginning of this year allowed private companies to sell and buy hard currencies with rates close to that of the spot market.
In the past, kerb dealers and traders in the exchange buisness risked harsh penalties ranging from long prison terms to amputations.
Kasab declined to say how much money a person can buy from state banks."The amount is decided by our potentials," he said.

The government decision follows a slump in the value of the dinar as a result of the delay in implementing a UN food-for-oil deal allowing Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy food and medicine.

The fall in the value of the dinar has brought harsh criticism from Baghdad's official media. Babel, owned by President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday, on Wednesday attacked traders, blaming them for the slump in the value of the local currency.

"Speculators and traders of crises are killing people (with their prices) sometimes because of the U.S. recent aggression against Iraq and sometimes because of the (U.S. President) Clinton's statements towards Iraq...," the paper said.
The U.S. last month fired two waves of missiles against Iraq as a punishment for its military support of one Kurdish rival against the other in the north of the country.

Prior to U.N. trade sanctions, imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, the dinar was an oil-backed currency worth 3.1 dollars. When Iraq entered talks with U.N. on partial oil sales early in the year the dollar was worth more than 3,000 dinars.

"This is the first time that banks are allowed to sell (hard currency) to people. In the past they use to sell them to only (government-licensed) importers, students (sent by the government to study abroad) and the sick sent by the state to recive their treatment abroad," Kasab said.
